Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design 2026

# CB-VER: A Stable Foundation for Modular Network Control Plane Verification

Dexin Zhang *, Timothy Alberdingk Thijm †, David Walker *, Aarti Gupta *

*Princeton University, Princeton, USA, {dz7903,dpw,aartig}@cs.princeton.edu †tthijm.fmcad26@gmail.com

Abstract—Network operators are often interested in verifying eventually-stable properties of network control planes: properties of control plane states that hold eventually, and hold forever thereafter, provided the operating environment remains unchanged. In this work, we introduce CB-VER, a new modular framework for verifying such properties, based on the key idea of a converges-before graph (CB-graph for short). Given userprovided specifications for each network component, CB-VER checks the necessary requirements in parallel using an SMT solver and automatically generates a CB-graph. Verification succeeds if all requirements are met and the generated CB-graph connects all nodes in a network. We formalize our verification algorithm in the Lean theorem prover and prove its soundness. Moreover, the generated CB-graph can be used to determine fault tolerance properties of the network. We also consider the inverted problem: Given a connected CB-graph, we can automatically synthesize suitable component specifications by formulating the problem as a Constrained Horn Clause (CHC) problem that ensures the given correctness property. We evaluate the performance of CB-VER and the synthesis tool (along with comparison to other tools) to demonstrate that they can successfully verify expressive properties on a range of benchmarks. Index Terms—Networks, control plane verification, modular verification, invariants, invariant synthesis.

I. INTRODUCTION

Network control planes define the paths to forward traffic from routers to destinations, using distributed routing protocols (such as BGP, OSPF, RIP, and others) that are configured by network operators. In today’s large cloud provider networks, these configuration files can be extremely challenging to update correctly due to the network’s scale and complexity [2]. To verify that updates are correct and prevent network outages, researchers have developed control plane verification techniques [3], [11]–[13], [21], [25], [36], [37], [42]–[44] (discussed in detail, §VI). However, they often fail to scale on large networks, due to the inherent verification complexity. Consequently, there is growing interest in modularly verifying the correctness of networks’ control planes [6], [8], [25], [39]. In modular network verification, a correctness property like eventually-stable reachability (“router X eventually always has a path to a destination D”) is decomposed into subproblems on the components of the network. These subproblems check that each component is correct with respect to a suitable component specification, assuming that all other components also respect their component specifications. This modular approach scales much better than monolithic verification, but requires users to supply correct component specifications for

each component. Writing such a component specification can be challenging and burdensome: for example, Lightyear [39] requires users to specify invariants and a network path (along which routing messages flow) to prove a liveness property; Timepiece [8] requires users to specify a function describing how each component’s routing state changes at each time instant, and applies only to synchronous schedules. We have developed a new system CB-VER for modular network verification with distinct advantages over prior work. Unlike Lightyear [39], properties that depend on route preferences can be proven by CB-VER, and users do not have to supply a path – a supporting graph is inferred automatically. Unlike Timepiece [8], CB-VER is sound for all schedules, and users need not refer to exact times in their specifications. In addition, CB-VER automatically infers the degree of fault tolerance of any verified property, a key feature of interest to network engineers, not provided by other modular systems. The approach in CB-VER is to focus on eventually-stable correctness properties of network behavior, i.e., properties that hold at some future time and forever after that1. In addition to properties, every network router (node) v is associated with two component specifications, I(v) and Q(v). (These can be regarded as per-component annotations, which are common in deductive program verification [29], [30] in the form of permethod annotations.) Specifically, I overapproximates the set of states the node can enter at any time during the routing decision process, while Q overapproximates its eventuallystable states. Intuitively, I is similar to an invariant, and we call Q an abstract convergence set because it overapproximates the states to which the network node converges. The key idea in CB-VER is to automatically infer a converges-before graph (CB-graph)2, which serves to provide a witness for the network convergence process. Rather than require a user to provide a CB-graph, CB-VER automatically generates it from the user-supplied annotations (I, Q). For verification to succeed, the generated CB-graph must connect all nodes to the origin(s) of the routing process. We have formalized this theory in Lean [34] and proved that our algorithm is sound with respect to a standard asynchronous network semantics. In addition, the CB-graph generated by CB-VER has the maximal connectivity for the given I and Q: if edges of a CB-

graph fail, then connectivity is reduced. Hence, by analyzing the connectivity of the CB-graph, it is possible to determine the degree of fault tolerance of any proven property—a key concern for network engineers building resilient systems. Finally, we also consider the inverted problem: when a connected CB-graph is user-supplied, can suitable component specifications I and Q be synthesized automatically for a given property? We use our theory to formulate this as a CHC (Constrained Horn Clause) problem [14], and use an off-theshelf CHC solver for demonstrating this capability. Summary of Contributions.

• Modular control plane verification: We present the theory (§II) and algorithm for CB-VER (§III). Given component specifications (I, Q) and target properties, it generates and checks per-node and per-edge verification conditions (VCs) in parallel using Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) solvers [18], and performs a lightweight global graph connectivity check to prove correctness.

• CB-graphs for sound modular reasoning (§II-D): CB- VER automatically generates a CB-graph, which provides a structure for well-founded induction in reasoning about correctness. We formalize our theory of abstract convergence and the verification algorithm in Lean [34] and prove its soundness.

• Automated fault analysis via CB-graphs (§II-E): We show that if the generated CB-graph is connected despite k arbitrarily selected CB-graph edge failures, then the verified property is k-fault tolerant.

• Automated synthesis of component specifications (§IV): When a connected CB-graph is given, we can automatically synthesize suitable I and Q for each node by formulating a CHC problem based on our theory.

• Evaluation (§V): We have developed prototype implementations of CB-VER and the synthesis tool (CB-2IQ), and evaluate them on a range of benchmarks, illustrating the expressiveness of the properties, the performance, and comparison with other tools.

In comparison to the most closely related modular verifiers (more details in §VI), our framework focuses on a broad, new category of eventually-stable properties, has different (simpler, we would argue) component specifications, adds failure analysis, and comes with an additional tool for component specification synthesis.

II. CB-VER: THE THEORY

A. Network Model and Semantics

The network control plane is a set of routers that exchange messages with each other about available paths (routes) to a destination using standard routing protocols such as BGP, OSPF, RIP [31], [32], [35]. Each router maintains a route that is most preferred among all available ones from its neighbors (with the preference relation depending on the protocol). Routers can modify or drop routes from their neighbors during message transfer, based on the configuration of export and im-

port policies. 3 They repeatedly and asynchronously exchange routes, and the network control plane (hopefully) converges with every router selecting its best route to a destination. We represent network control planes using a standard network model, inspired by routing algebras [24], [38], where each network instance considers one destination prefix (i.e., a set of IP addresses). This model has been applied to a wide range of routing protocols used in practice, including BGP, RIP, OSPF. Formally, a network instance is a 5-tuple N = (G, R, init, f, ⊕), where:

• G = (V, E) is a simple, finite directed graph. The nodes V are routers and directed edges E ⊆V × V are links.

• R is the set of routing messages, or simply routes, that can be exchanged between nodes. R varies according to the protocol; ∞∈R (invalid route) is used when no route is selected.

• init : V →R is a function that maps each node v ∈V to its initial route init(v) ∈R, which is the route that originates from v or is imported from external sources at a border node. It is ∞if there are no routes originated or imported at node v.

• f : E →(R →R) maps each edge (u, v) ∈E to a transfer function f(e) : R →R (also written as fe). For instance, f(u,v) is the transfer function for routes sent from u to v, based on the configuration of export and import policies.

• ⊕: R × R →R is a binary associative, commutative and selective function (the merge function) that selects the best route between two routes. It is defined by each protocol; ∞is required to be the least preferred route. Encoding network model in SMT. Modeling routing protocols using SMT theories is a well-understood process [11]. The set of routes R is represented as a record of fields, which depend on the specific protocol, and each field is encoded as a sort (i.e., type) in some first-order theory [9]. The other components — init, f, ⊕— are modeled as expressions and formulas in first-order theories. Full details of our SMT encoding of the BGP protocol are available in an extended version of this paper [47]. Asynchronous schedules and fairness. To model an asynchronous network, we follow the approach of Üresin and Dubois [40] and Daggitt et al. [17]. In this model, times are natural numbers T = N, and a schedule for a network N is a pair (α, β) with:

1) An activation function α : T →2V that maps a time t to a set of routers α(t) activated at that time. 2) A data flow function β : E →(T →T) that defines the time taken to traverse each link e = (u, v). If t1 = β(e)(t2) (also written βe(t2)), the route sent by u at time t1 will arrive at v at time t2. Messages must be received after they are sent and hence t2 > t1 in all cases. These asynchronous schedules can model arbitrary delay, loss, duplication, or reordering of any message in transit.

3In our model, we use the term "route" to refer to both states and messages.

When proving soundness, we additionally assume that nodes and edges are not failed: they activate infinitely often and send/receive up-to-date messages infinitely often (formal definitions are presented in the extended version [47]). Such schedules with no failures are called fair schedules. In §II-E, we consider tolerance under edge failures; elsewhere, we assume a schedule is fair unless stated otherwise. Network semantics and concrete convergence. The network semantics of N with respect to a schedule S = (α, β) is defined as the following function σS : V × T →R. (This is the same as in prior work on routing algebras [17].)

σS(v, t) =

At t = 0, each node v selects its initial route init(v). Henceforth, if v is activated at time t (i.e., v ∈α(t)), it will select the best route among all routes received from its neighbors (possibly delayed). Otherwise, its route remains the same as at time t −1. For a given schedule S and network N, we say node v (concretely) converges to r if ∃τ. ∀t ≥τ, σS(v, t) = r. In other words, v converges to r if σS(v, t) is equal to r for some t and forever after. At the network level, we say the network semantics σS converges to σ∗ S : V →R if v converges to σ∗ S(v) for each node v. Such a state σ∗ S is called a converged state of the network. Note that a network may have multiple converged states for different schedules S (this can happen in real networks [15]), or it may have no converged state (e.g., it may oscillate between a set of states [23]).

B. Running Example and Correctness Properties

Consider a simple network, shown in Fig. 1, with four nodes running the BGP routing protocol. A network operator would like to prove that node E has a route to destination node A after the network has converged, and moreover that the route goes through B rather than C (perhaps the former route is less costly than the latter). To implement this preference, the network operator uses BGP’s local preference mechanism, setting the local preference attribute to 300 when E imports routes from B, and leaving it as the default value 100 everywhere else. When node E receives routes from multiple neighbors, it chooses the route with the highest local preference (in this case, the route from B with value 300 over the route from

C with value 100). The routing process starts with node A originating a route by announcing a route to itself, and no other node having an initial route to A. In the rest of the paper, we will use this as a running example to illustrate key ideas and concepts in our theory. Formal definition of correctness properties. A user-provided correctness property Y : V →2R maps each node v to some predicate (formula) Y (v) on routes R. Our theory supports verification of eventually-stable properties associated with such state predicates Y . More formally, we verify that for all schedules S:

∀v. ∃τ. ∀t ≥τ. σS(v, t) ∈Y (v).

Running example. In our example, suppose we have the following properties of interest:

• Y1(E): Will node E be able to reach A?

• Y2(E): Will node E select a path to A using a route from node B rather than from node C? The first property Y1(E) expresses a simple reachability property, while the second Y2(E) captures a preference property. The user is interested in checking that these properties hold at some point and forever after (provided changes to the operating environment do not occur, e.g., configuration/policy changes). To express these properties in terms of a route state s at E, we define a routing field aspath(s) that represents the AS path of s, represented as a list of AS numbers of routers in the routing path so far:

Y1(E) = {s | s ̸= ∞}

Y2(E) = {s | s ̸= ∞∧C /∈aspath(s)}

Note that the predicates here refer implicitly to the destination A, i.e., all routes s are interpreted as routes to A (and s ̸= ∞ represents some available route to A). Expressiveness of Properties. CB-VER requires properties Y to be written as per-node predicates over routes R, to enable modular verification. However, global properties or path-dependent properties can also be expressed in CB-VER in a modular form through decomposition or the introduction of ghost variables and ghost code. For example, global connectivity (i.e., connectivity between all or certain nodes) can be decomposed into single-destination connectivity per destination d. For each d, we can define property Y (v) to be “v can reach the destination d” (as shown in the running example above for a single destination A), and then verify separately for all/certain destinations d. For path-dependent properties, we can introduce ghost fields that are updated along the path. For example, to verify that any route selected by v must go through a node in the set of nodes W, one can add a Boolean ghost field ViaW that is set to true when a route is imported by a node in W. We can then define Y (v) = {s | ViaW(s) = true}. Use of ghost fields is also common in deductive program verification [29], [30]. We note that properties beyond path-dependent properties, such as relational properties between arbitrary routers, may require some heavy instrumentation (e.g., via a product construction).

C. Abstracting Convergence for Proving Correctness CB-VER requires the user to provide an annotation Q, which we call an abstract convergence set. Formally, Q : V → 2R, which maps each node v to some predicate (formula) Q(v) on routes. Given a specific network instance and (fair) schedule S, we say that σS(v, t) abstractly converges to Q(v) if:

∃τ. ∀t ≥τ, σS(v, t) ∈Q(v).

Note that if σS(v, t) abstractly converges to Q(v), this schedule may not actually converge to a single concrete state in Q(v), but if it does, then the concrete converged route σ∗ S(v) must be included in the set Q(v). We say a node v abstractly converges to Q(v) if σS(v, t) abstractly converges to Q(v) for all schedules S. In the rest of the paper, we say “abstractly converges to Q(v)” to signify that we are interested in reasoning about convergence to a set of states, rather than convergence to a single state. This abstraction of convergence via an overapproximation is novel to our approach and provides crucial benefits. The user does not have to specify exactly which state a node converges to, only a set containing the concrete state(s); moreover, if a network does not actually converge to a single state, but loops within a subset of the states characterized by Q, violations of expected properties in such states will still provide useful feedback to users. (Other related work on guaranteeing (unique) convergence in routing protocols [16], [17] is orthogonal to our work, see more details in §VI. ) Our two-step strategy for proving correctness is to (1) establish that all nodes v abstractly converge to Q(v), and (2) for each node v, check that every route in Q(v) satisfies Y (v). If any step fails, then verification fails. The second step is easy to do: we use an SMT solver to check the validity of Q(v) ⇒Y (v) (where ⇒denotes propositional implication). However, the first step is more challenging, and is discussed in the next subsection. Running example. We consider the second step for our running example. To prove Y1(E), it suffices to choose Q1(v) = {s | s ̸= ∞} for v ∈{A, B, C, E}. Note that Q1(E) = Y1(E) here, so the second step holds trivially. However, to prove Y2(E), we need a stronger component specification Q2(E) (lp(s) represents local preference of the route s, and len(s) represents the length of the AS path of s):

Q2(E) = {s | s ̸= ∞∧lp(s) = 300∧len(s) = 2∧C /∈aspath(s)}

Furthermore, the component specifications Q2(v) at other nodes v must also be more specific to affirm the absence of node C along the route transferred from A through B to E:

Q2(A) = {s | s ̸= ∞∧lp(s) = 100 ∧len(s) = 0 ∧C /∈aspath(s)} Q2(B) = {s | s ̸= ∞∧lp(s) = 100 ∧len(s) = 1 ∧C /∈aspath(s)} Q2(C) = {s | s ̸= ∞∧lp(s) = 100 ∧len(s) = 1}

Given the above Q(v) component specifications for each node v, it is straightforward to check that for each property, Q1(E) ⇒Y1(E) and Q2(E) ⇒Y2(E).

D. CB-graphs: Key Structure for Sound Reasoning

Recall that we still need to establish the first step: that all nodes v abstractly converge to their given specifications Q(v), i.e., Q(v) is a sound abstract convergence set for v. To help with this, a user also provides a specification I(v) for each node v — we call I an invariant. To show that I(v) is sound, we check that it overapproximates the set of routes that node v selects at any time during the routing process. CB-VER performs additional checks to ensure that the user-provided specifications I(v) and Q(v) are sound. A justification at node v could depend on the specifications of its neighbor nodes, but not if they, in turn, are justified recursively by the specifications at v. This circular reasoning would clearly be unsound. To ensure soundness of our theory, we introduce the CBgraph. Intuitively, a CB-graph provides a witness that all nodes v in the network abstractly converge to their Q(v). Formally, a CB-graph consists of CB-roots and CB-edges, which are defined as follows:

• CB-roots: a non-empty subset of nodes w ∈V , where each w must select a route σS(w, t) ∈Q(w) at any time t (starting from t = 0), for any schedule S. In practice, a node that originates routes as a destination, or acts as a border node (that imports routes from external sources) is a CB-root.

• CB-edges: a subset of directed edges (u, v) in the network, such that for any schedule S, if u selects a route σS(u, t1) ∈Q(u) at time t1, and transfers this route along edge (u, v), then v must select a route σS(v, t2) ∈Q(v), where t2 is the time that v receives and merges u’s route.

Running example. Fig. 2 shows the CB-graphs generated by CB-VER for our running example with component specifications I1, Q1 and I2, Q2, respectively. The destination node A is a CB-root in both, and the red directed arrows show the CB-edges. The node A is a CB-root because it originates a route: the routes at A at t = 0 and at all times thereafter belong to the component specifications Q1(A) and Q2(A). As an example of a CB-edge, consider the edge BE in the network with the I1, Q1 component specifications. If node B has a route in Q1(B) (i.e., if it has a route at all), then a route transfer from B to E will definitely result in E having a route in Q1(E) after the transfer. Critically, this is true regardless of which other messages may have reached E earlier (i.e., for any state in I1(E) that node E was in earlier). Thus, the edge BE is a CB-edge. In fact, every directed edge in the

<!-- Page 5 -->


network is a CB-edge for I1, Q1. This is because no routes are dropped along any edge; thus, transfer of a route along each edge necessarily establishes Q1 at the receiving node. As an example of an edge that is not a CB-edge, consider the edge CE for the I2, Q2 component specifications. Suppose node C has a route in Q2(C), and transfers this route to node E. Suppose E does not have any route before this transfer, perhaps due to delays along the BE edge. Then, as a result of transfer from C, node E will select this route where the path includes C. However, this route does not belong to Q2(E), as defined earlier (since its path includes C). Therefore, the CE edge is not a CB-edge. Connected CB-graphs. We say that a CB-graph is connected if every node v in the network is itself a CB-root or has a path of CB-edges from some CB-root w to v. The following important theorem states that a connected CB-graph provides a basis for reasoning about convergence. (A proof sketch of the theorem and Lean formalizations appear in the extended version [47]; a formal proof has been mechanized in Lean.4)

Theorem 1 (Connected CB-graph Theorem). If a CB-graph for Q is connected, then all nodes v in the network abstractly converge to Q(v).

Note that we do not require a CB-graph to be acyclic – this provides flexibility while ensuring soundness. Any connected CB-graph must have a connected acyclic subgraph that can serve as a witness for all nodes v in the network to abstractly converge to their Q(v). More importantly, we note that CB-VER does not require a user to provide a CB-graph to establish abstract convergence; it automatically generates a maximal CB-graph and checks that it is connected. More details are presented in §III-A, where CB- VER maximally identifies each node as a CB-root and each edge as a CB-edge, provided they meet certain requirements.

E. CB-graphs and Fault tolerance

In this subsection, we consider edge failures and the correctness of properties under at most k edge failures. An edge is considered failed if it does not deliver any messages sent after a certain time (a formal definition is shown in the Lean formalizations in the extended version [47]). We say that a CBgraph is k-fail-connected, if it remains connected regardless of which combination of k CB-edges is removed.

Theorem 2 (Fault tolerance theorem). If a CB-graph for Q is k-fail-connected, then for any schedule S where at most k edges are failed, all nodes v in the network abstractly converge to Q(v) and the network N is k-fault tolerant.

Example for fault-tolerance. Consider Fig. 3, which shows a network with 13 routers and 3 ASs (taken from a Batfish tutorial [45]). Suppose a user is interested in checking reachability to Houston, and provides Q such that it includes any route except ∞. The generated CB-graph is also shown in the figure.

III. FROM THEORY TO MODULAR TOOL: CB-VER

We now describe how we use our theory of abstract convergence to develop a modular verifier CB-VER.

A. CB-VER Algorithm

CB-VER generates and checks Verification Conditions (VCs) on nodes and edges in the network. These are summarized in Fig. 4, where each row shows a different VC set based on their role (explained below), and the respective formula generated by CB-VER. The formulas capture conditions on arbitrary routes su and sv at nodes u and v, respectively. The conditions are expressed in terms of the network model (i.e., with operations init, f, ⊕for the network instance), component specifications (Q, I), and correctness property (Y ) provided by the user. For each of these VCs, CB-VER invokes an SMT solver (e.g., Z3 [18]) to check its validity. If the check fails, the solver provides a counterexample, i.e., values of su, sv where the formula is false. The first three VCs are regarded as essential VCs, because if any of them fail, then CB-VER immediately reports failure. They serve the following roles:

• Checking invariant specification I: V CInit and V CInv together ensure that the user-provided component specification I is an inductive invariant at each node v. As shown, V CInit performs a base check on every node v, to ensure that the initial route init(v) is in I(v). V CInv performs an inductive check for every edge (u, v): if a route su is in I(u), then the route sv selected by v after its transfer-and-merge must also be in I(v). Here, the subformula sv⊕fu,v(su) represents the new route at node v after the merge (⊕) of its existing route sv and the transferred route (f(u,v)(su)) from neighbor u.

• Checking correctness property Y : V CProp ensures that every route in the abstract convergence specification Q(v) satisfies Y (v). This is needed for checking the correctness of the eventual-stability property.

CB-VER requires that a user provide Q, I, but it alleviates some burden by constructing a CB-graph for Q. It checks two VCs, V CCBroot and V CCBedge, on all nodes and edges to identify CB-roots and CB-edges, respectively.

• Identifying CB-roots: V CCBroot(v) checks that init(v) is in Q(v), and for every incoming edge (u, v) with su as some arbitrary selected state at node u (i.e., su ∈I(u)), the route selected by v after transfer-and-merge must also belong to Q(v). If V CCBroot(v) is valid, then node v is a CB-root.

• Identifying CB-edges: V CCBedge((u, v)) checks that if su is in Q(u), and if sv is some arbitrary selected route at node v (i.e., sv ∈I(v)), then the route selected by v after transfer-and-merge must belong to Q(v). If V CCBedge((u, v)) is valid, then edge (u, v) is a CB-edge.

Putting it all together. The complete verification algorithm including generation and checking of the VCs is shown (as pseudocode) in Fig. 5. It takes a network N, correctness property Y , and component specifications I, Q as inputs, and produces output Correct or Fail (with counterexamples). The algorithm has two phases. In phase 1 (lines 2-17), CB- VER generates and checks all VCs on the nodes and edges in parallel. If any of the essential VCs (V CInit, V CInv, V CProp) is not valid, then CB-VER reports Fail immediately, along with a counterexample for debugging purposes. The other two VCs (V CCBroot, V CCBedge) are not essential in the sense that CB- VER does not report Fail immediately. If a VC in V CCBroot or V CCBedge is not valid, the associated node or edge is not added to the corresponding set (in phase 1), and CB-VER will save the counterexample for later use. We have shown (via a Lean formalization) that CB-VER is also complete when all transfer functions f are strictly monotonic (i.e., x < y ⇒f(x) < f(y), where x < y is defined as x ̸= y and x ⊕y = x) and < is a well-ordering relation on R. However, CB-VER is not complete in general for arbitrary routing protocols. An example that shows incompleteness, inspired by Daggitt and Griffin’s work [16], is presented in an extended version of this paper [47]. Intuitively, CB- VER is complete when the network has a “simple pattern of convergence”, where the routing tree (or an acyclic graph) in the converged state can be used as a CB-graph. Our evaluations (§V) show that CB-VER can successfully verify many networks in practice, in which all networks have such a pattern of convergence.

B. Annotation Design and Debugging Methodology

To use CB-VER in practice, a user needs to provide suitable I and Q that can be proven sound, and Q(v) must be sufficient to establish the desired property Y (v). To specify such I and Q, a user typically starts from the property Y and tries specifying Q as a subset of Y , and also a superset of the converged routes. This can often be expressed as a conjunction of Y with some strengthening clauses. After finding Q, the user can try specifying I as a superset of all possible routes selected at any time – typically expressed as a disjunction of Q with some "pre-convergence" routes. 5

Starting from an initial set of annotations, which may be incorrect or inadequate, the user can use an iterative debugging process using CB-VER. When verification fails, the counterexamples from failed VCs provide feedback for userassisted error debugging. Thanks to the modularity of CB- VER, each VC violation is localized, i.e., it is caused by the configurations or specifications of a certain node or edge. For example, when V CCBedge fails, the SMT solver will generate concrete routes su, sv such that su ∈Q(u) ∧sv ∈I(v) but sv ⊕f(u,v)(su) = s′ v /∈Q(v). Based on their beliefs (or knowledge) about su, sv, s′ v, a user can strengthen Q(u), I(v) to exclude su, sv, or weaken Q(v) to include s′ v. In the extended version of this paper [47], we describe a user-assisted debugging process with all cases and illustrate it with an example. It is also possible that the transfer function f(u,v)

IV. SYNTHESIS OF COMPONENT SPECIFICATIONS

In this section, we consider a different variation of the verification problem, where a user may have an idea of a CBgraph, but would like to automatically synthesize the component specifications I, Q, in order to prove the property Y of interest. This is often the case in practice for highly structured networks such as those found in data centers: for instance, fat-tree topologies [4] are configured to use routes along welldefined valley-free paths. In such structured topologies and policies, a CB-graph often corresponds to a BFS (breadth-first search) graph from the destination. Given a CB-graph, our approach for synthesis of the component specifications is based on Constrained Horn Clauses (CHC). CHC formulations are widely used in program verification and invariant synthesis [14], [22], [26]. We follow their notation in definitions shown below.

Definition 1. A constrained Horn clause (CHC) rule has one of the following two forms:

∀x1, · · · , xn. ϕ(⃗x) ∧R1(⃗x) ∧· · · Rn(⃗x) ⇒Rn+1(⃗x)

∀x1, · · · , xn. ϕ(⃗x) ∧R1(⃗x) ∧· · · Rn(⃗x) ⇒False

where ϕ is an interpreted formula (over some first-order theory) and each Ri is an uninterpreted predicate. Note that the variables in each CHC rule (x1, · · · , xn) are universally quantified — these quantifiers are implicit when not shown.

A CHC system is a conjunction of CHC rules. A solution of a CHC system is an interpretation of predicates Ri (typically in the form of formulas in some first-order theory) such that all CHC rules are valid. A CHC solver (such as Spacer/Z3 [27]) searches for a solution; a CHC system is called infeasible if no such solution exists. Formulating component specification synthesis in CHC. We formulate CHC rules based on the VCs we showed earlier, but where Iv, Qv are now uninterpreted predicates to be solved, rather than interpreted predicates provided by a user. The CBgraph (CBRoot ⊆V , CBEdge ⊆E) is provided by the user, property Yv and network logic (initv, f(u,v)) are interpreted (based on the network configurations). The complete CHC system for the network component specification synthesis problem is shown in Fig. 6. For each VC set in Fig. 4, we formulate a CHC rule for each member of the set (a node, edge, CB-root or CB-edge). Note that V CCBroot results in two CHC rules to conform to the definition of CHCs. Prototype tool CB-2IQ. We have implemented CB-2IQ based on the above CHC formulation. Our tool uses BFS traversal to check that the user-provided CB-graph is connected. If a CHC solution exists, it corresponds to an interpretation of the Iv, Qv predicates that make all CHC rules valid, which establishes successful verification due to all VCs passing. An off-the-shelf CHC solver typically works with all CHC rules together in a non-modular way; we leave modular synthesis to future work.

V. IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION

We have developed a prototype implementation of CB-VER, using Batfish [20] to extract the network model from Cisco and Juniper configurations. The tool is implemented in C#, using Microsoft’s Zen library [33] and SMT solver Z3 [18]. The CB- 2IQ prototype translates the CHC rules (Fig. 6) into SMTLib format [10] and uses Spacer [26], [27] (version 4.13.0, part of Z3) to solve the CHC problem. Since Spacer does not support the theory of sequences (needed for modeling aspath), we used a slightly simplified BGP model for the CB-2IQ evaluations. In this simplified model, we replace the field of AS-paths with an abstraction (its length) and encode communities as a boolean array (assuming the communities are among a few pre-determined values). While CB-2IQ is less expressive than CB-VER, our evaluations are not affected since the transfer function and property involve only simplified fields in all benchmark instances. Evaluation Goals. We seek to answer the following questions.

• RQ1: Expressiveness. Is CB-VER able to verify a variety of properties for a diverse collection of networks, including data center fat-trees [4] as well as other realworld topologies and policies?

• RQ2: Performance of verification. How well does CB-VER perform as a verifier? Does it scale on large networks and complex configurations?

• RQ3: Usability of fault tolerance analysis. Is CB-VER able to perform a push-button fault tolerance analysis based on CB-graph? What information can users gain from this analysis?

• RQ4: Performance of component specification synthesis. How well does CB-2IQ perform in practice? Comparison of CB-VER with other tools. For a baseline comparison, we have implemented a monolithic SMT-based verifier (MS) based on the algorithm in Minesweeper [11]. We also compare CB-VER with Timepiece [8], using an artifact [7], [8] (with their user-provided component specifications). Lightyear tool [39] is not available (confirmed by the authors). We note that since the inputs (properties and annotations) of CB-VER are different from those in other

tools (MS, Timepiece), and they require different levels of user effort, it is not possible to perform a fair apples-toapples comparison. However, our goal is to focus on the same properties (such as reachability) that are of interest to network operators. We report on the success and runtimes of different tools to provide information about their efficacy and practicality, which can be viewed as more indicative of their capabilities rather than a quantitative assessment.

A. Benchmarks and Setup We worked with three sets of benchmarks, described below.6

(1) Synthetic fattrees. We use parameterized fattree networks (20–2000 nodes) with auto-generated configurations in Cisco’s format (via Batfish frontend [20]) (with about 50-300 lines of code per node). We verify the following four properties often used in datacenters:

• Reachability: all nodes must have reachability to a fixed destination;

• PathLength: the selected route at all nodes (to a fixed destination) must be the shortest path;

• ValleyFree: the selected route at all nodes (to a fixed destination) must not be a valley (up-down-up);

• Hijack: certain routes from an external "hijacker" node must be blocked from the internal network. We remark that Timepiece [8] used the same properties, and Lightyear does not support the PathLength and ValleyFree properties. Additional details with full specifications used in CB-VER are provided in the extended version [47]. (2) Internet2. The Internet2 benchmark [1] is a real wide-area network with over 100,000 lines of Juniper configurations. It has 293 nodes (10 internal routers, 283 external neighbors).7

We use a snapshot of Internet2’s configurations [43] that have been reported to violate some properties. 8 We consider the

VI. RELATED WORK

Modular Network Verification. CB-VER improves upon related modular verifiers [6], [8], [25], [39] in various aspects. RCDC [25] was a pioneer in modular network verification, but was customized for checking invariants of Azure data centers, not for other settings. Kirigami [6] requires a user to exactly identify the concrete converged state of a network, a difficult task requiring exact knowledge of network internals. Lightyear [39] is able to verify safety and liveness properties, but not those that involve path lengths or path preferences. It requires users to provide invariants (for safety) and a specific path and path constraints (for liveness), thereby placing a higher burden on users than in CB-VER, which automatically generates a CB-graph. Timepiece [8] requires the user to provide component specifications as functions that describe how each component’s routing state changes over all time instants. While it can support more expressive properties (also expressed as functions over time) than CB-VER, this comes at the cost of higher user burden. Furthermore, Timepiece considers only a synchronous schedule, whereas CB-VER is proven sound under asynchronous network semantics. Control plane verification. Our work is more broadly related to verification of network control plane configurations [3], [11]–[13], [21], [36], [37], [42]–[44]. Bagpipe [43] and Minesweeper [11] use SMT-based verification, but are monolithic verifiers. ARC [21] and Tiramisu [3] reduce verification problems to efficient graph analyses, but do not handle all network features. Plankton [36], Hoyan [44], and Expresso [42] combine a mix of symbolic analyses and simulation to improve scalability. Bonsai [12] uses symmetry-based abstractions, Shapeshifter [13] uses abstractions on routing fields, and ACORN [37] uses route nondeterminism to improve scalability — these abstractions are orthogonal to our work. Reasoning about convergence. Other efforts focus on network

routing protocols, to check convergence and identify conditions under which (unique) convergence is guaranteed [17], [24], [38]. However, practical networks often use rich routing policies that do not conform to these conditions. Furthermore, these efforts do not target checking network- and policyspecific routing path properties for given network instances. Program verification and invariant synthesis. CHC solvers have been widely used in program verification and invariant synthesis [14], [22], [26]. In addition to invariants I, we use specifications Q to prove properties that are eventually-stable.

VII. CONCLUSIONS

We developed CB-VER, a new framework for verifying eventually-stable control plane properties in a modular way, based on abstracting convergence and automatically generating a converges-before (CB) graph from given component specifications. We proved our verifier correct in Lean, and illustrate its benefits in fault tolerance analysis. We evaluated CB-VER on a collection of benchmark examples, illustrating its expressiveness and performance. Given a CB-graph, we also performed automated component specification synthesis and show its effectiveness in practice.
